name: Robert Meisenbach
bio: Robert Meisenbach was a University of California student charged with felony assault with a deadly weapon — accused by police of starting the May 1960 anti-HUAC demonstration at San Francisco City Hall, where students were fire-hosed down the steps. The lone person prosecuted from that protest, he was acquitted in May 1961.
charges: Assault with a deadly weapon — the anti-HUAC San Francisco City Hall protest

name: John Hardy
bio: John Hardy was a SNCC voter-registration worker who, after a registrar struck him on the head with a pistol in Tylertown (Walthall County), Mississippi in 1961, was himself arrested on a breach-of-peace charge. The U.S. Justice Department sued to block his prosecution.
charges: Breach of the peace — SNCC voter-registration work
convicted: Arrested 1961; Justice Dept. sought to enjoin the prosecution

name: Brenda Travis
bio: Brenda Travis was a 16-year-old arrested in August 1961 in a sit-in at the McComb, Mississippi Greyhound bus station and sentenced to a year in reform school. Her punishment helped spark the October 1961 walkout by McComb high-school students.
charges: Sit-in / breach of peace — McComb bus-station desegregation

name: Robert Zellner
bio: Robert Zellner was a SNCC field secretary — the only white participant in the Oct. 4, 1961 McComb, Mississippi student demonstration — who was beaten by a mob on the courthouse steps, jailed two days, and charged with breach of the peace and contributing to the delinquency of minors.
charges: Breach of the peace; contributing to the delinquency of minors — McComb demonstration
sentence: Jailed and charged for the McComb protest

name: Robert F. Williams
bio: Robert F. Williams was the president of the Union County (Monroe), North Carolina NAACP and an advocate of armed Black self-defense. In 1961, amid racial violence around the Monroe desegregation protests, he was indicted on a charge of kidnapping a white couple — a charge he and supporters denounced as a frame-up — and fled the FBI manhunt, receiving asylum in Cuba.
charges: Kidnapping (state) + federal flight to avoid prosecution — denounced as a civil-rights frame-up
sentence: Indicted in the Monroe frame-up; exiled to Cuba

name: Richard Crowder
bio: Richard Crowder was one of the Monroe, North Carolina defendants held in high bail on the kidnapping charge arising from the August 1961 racial conflict around the Monroe desegregation pickets; he was scheduled for trial on Oct. 30, 1961.
convicted: Jailed on high bail; tried October 1961
sentence: Jailed pending trial in the Monroe case

name: Harold Reap
bio: Harold Reap was one of the defendants jailed on high bail in Monroe, North Carolina on the kidnapping charge growing out of the 1961 racial violence around the Monroe desegregation protests; he was set for trial on Oct. 30, 1961.
convicted: Jailed on high bail; tried October 1961
sentence: Jailed pending trial in the Monroe case

name: John Lowery
bio: John Lowery was one of the Monroe, North Carolina defendants held on the kidnapping charge that arose from the August 1961 racial conflict around the Monroe desegregation pickets, scheduled for trial on Oct. 30, 1961.
convicted: Jailed on high bail; tried October 1961
sentence: Jailed pending trial in the Monroe case

name: Mae Mallory
bio: Mae Mallory was a 34-year-old civil-rights activist who had gone to Monroe, North Carolina to support Robert F. Williams. Arrested in Cleveland in October 1961, she was indicted on a North Carolina kidnapping charge and a federal fugitive-from-justice charge arising from the Monroe racial conflict, and fought extradition.
charges: Kidnapping (state) + federal fugitive from justice — the Monroe civil-rights frame-up
sentence: Jailed; resisting extradition to North Carolina

name: W. G. Anderson
bio: Dr. W. G. Anderson was the leader of the Albany Movement, the broad desegregation campaign in Albany, Georgia. He was among those arrested in the December 1961 mass demonstrations in which some 750 people — including Martin Luther King Jr. — were jailed.
charges: Civil-rights demonstration arrests — the Albany Movement
sentence: Jailed in the Albany Movement mass arrests

name: David Andrews
bio: The Rev. David Andrews was a Methodist minister who on Dec. 12, 1961 knelt at the White House fence in a 'direct act of civil disobedience' demanding the release of the imprisoned Morton Sobell. Ordered to move and refusing, he was arrested, and was freed in court the next day.
charges: Civil disobedience — White House protest for a political prisoner's release
sentence: Arrested at the White House protest

name: Martin Popper
bio: Martin Popper was a New York attorney and former secretary of the National Lawyers Guild, found guilty in 1961 on four counts of contempt of Congress and sentenced to six months in prison and a $500 fine for refusing, in 1959, to answer House Un-American Activities Committee questions on First Amendment grounds.
charges: Contempt of Congress — refusing to answer HUAC
sentence: Six months in prison and a $500 fine

name: Martin Chancey
bio: Martin Chancey was a Cleveland translation-service owner who had been tried and convicted with five others under the Smith Act in 1956 (the conviction reversed and the charges dismissed in 1958). In 1961 he was again subpoenaed before the House Un-American Activities Committee, which retained his business records — pursuit his supporters said was wrecking his livelihood.
charges: Smith Act (1956 conviction, reversed); renewed HUAC subpoena (1961)
sentence: Smith Act conviction reversed; later pursued by HUAC

name: Archie Brown
bio: Archie Brown was an executive-board member of ILWU Local 10 in San Francisco and an open Communist who, in May 1961, became the first person indicted under the Landrum-Griffin Act's provision barring Communists from holding union office — after his union elected him to office. His prosecution became the Supreme Court case United States v. Brown.
charges: Landrum-Griffin Act — a Communist holding union office
sentence: Faced up to a year and $10,000; challenged the law

name: Jose Maria Gastelum
bio: Jose Maria Gastelum was a Mexican-born Los Angeles resident, in the United States since 1921, who was arrested for deportation in 1956 on a charge of Communist Party membership in 'late 1949 or early 1950.' In 1961 the Supreme Court refused to review his case.
charges: Walter-McCarran Act deportation — alleged Communist Party membership
convicted: Deportation order; Supreme Court refused review (1961)
sentence: Under deportation order for alleged Communist membership

name: Ferdinand Smith
bio: Ferdinand Smith was a co-founder and national secretary of the National Maritime Union and the first Black member of the CIO executive council. Purged as a left-winger in 1948, he was forced out of the United States around 1951 under deportation proceedings as an 'undesirable' and 'subversive,' and died in Jamaica on Aug. 15, 1961.
sentence: Deported for his radical labor politics; died in exile
